accessAttack: A blocked pane is on-screen text, not a correlation. Concrete route: for p in $(tmux list-panes -a -F "#{pane_id}"); do tmux capture-pane -p -t $p | tail -6; done — six lines, aliased once, dumps the pending question for every harness at once with zero per-harness integration. Non-scripters get setw -g monitor-silence 45, a native tmux window flag raised the moment a pane goes quiet, or the iTerm2 per-tab activity dot; both are one-line setups. Even purely by hand, cycling 12 panes and reading the last lines is visiting several places and doing manual work (41-60), not correlating across sessions or across time (61-80): every answer is local to one pane and nothing has to be remembered.
impactAttack: B1 already ships for Claude, where most of the sessions in this model live, so B2 buys only the non-Claude tail. The note itself concedes Pi has no passive needs-input signal at all and that 85 is an average over eight quite different problems. A detector that is blank on some harnesses cannot license walking away, so the user keeps cycling panes exactly as before and gains earlier notice only on the harnesses that were already cheapest to instrument. The loss avoided is bounded by the gap to the next natural cycle, which at a desk is minutes rather than hours.

accessAttack: pgrep -fl "claude|codex|gemini|opencode|goose|droid|copilot" is one command that answers this for the entire fleet, and the briefing already lists ps as available. A dead session is additionally self-announcing in its own pane: the harness TUI is gone and you are looking at a bare shell prompt, a traceback, or a killed message. Finished-and-idle looks nothing like that, because the harness input box is still drawn and waiting. So the died-versus-finished distinction is a visible element per pane (0-20) plus one pgrep for the fleet (21-40). No correlation over time is involved, which is what 61-80 requires.
impactAttack: The stated harm is waiting on something that is never coming back, but nothing is actually lost: transcripts persist on disk and claude --resume, codex resume and their equivalents restart with context. The cost is idle minutes, and the action taken is restart it whether you learn now or on the next pane cycle. Crashes are also rare next to blocked and working states, so this changes a real decision occasionally rather than preventing concrete loss, and the shipped E1 stale flag already catches the long tail. The 77 is the drama of the word died, not the size of the recovered loss.

accessAttack: The one real route is the Claude Notification hook the briefing documents, pointed at a push service: curl -d blocked ntfy.sh/<topic> is a single line, and ntfy and Pushover are standard idioms in exactly this community. Tailscale plus the existing loopback dashboard is a second route. But both are setup projects rather than 30-second retrievals, they only exist for the one harness that already has a signal worth delivering, and the briefing states flatly that no harness delivers anything off the machine. I cannot honestly push this below 60. 72 rather than 75 only because the hook-plus-ntfy route is cheaper than the score implies and a competent developer really would write it. This access attack is weak and I am recording it as such.
impactAttack: Awareness without agency. B4, answering from the dashboard, is unbuilt and has been marked down three times, so a phone ping cannot unblock anything: the agent stays stalled until the user is back at a keyboard either way. The only behaviour it changes is returning sooner. And D9 on this same board concedes that unfiltered pings are the kind of absence that gets a tool uninstalled in week two, which is an admission that off-hours delivery gets muted rather than acted on. That caps it in the changes-a-real-decision band rather than the prevents-concrete-loss band, since reclaiming an idle 5-hour window by cutting a lunch short is a decision, not a rescued loss.

accessAttack: Two concrete native routes. First, setw -g monitor-silence 60 with set -g visual-bell on: tmux flags the window the instant a pane stops emitting, which is the state change in question, delivered unprompted without being asked — 0-20 for anyone already in tmux, and this user runs panes. Second, the Claude Notification hook the briefing documents, pointed at osascript -e display notification or terminal-notifier, is a one-line settings edit that reproduces the shipped macOS popup exactly. iTerm2 and GNOME Terminal both ship per-tab activity indicators for free. The 70 is also importing B2 engineering cost, detecting state changes across nine harnesses, into a number that is defined to measure the user route.
impactAttack: The note refutes its own outcome: off macOS this is a browser notification that still needs an open tab. A user with the dashboard tab open is already positioned to glance at it, so the ping replaces a glance rather than changing a decision, and the claimed outcome of stopping the polling is not achieved on the majority of platforms. Across 3-12 sessions a state-change notifier also fires often enough that the realistic end state is a muted channel, which is precisely why D9 exists on this board. Convenience delivered promptly is still convenience.

accessAttack: tmux capture-pane -p -t <pane> | tail -20, or the same one-line loop that answers B2, prints the completion text for the fleet. The finished-versus-waiting distinction is decided by whether the last thing on screen is a summary or a question: a local read of one pane, no correlation. Note also that nobody read it is not information Cargento holds either. With E6 dismissals unbuilt it can only infer idle-after-completion, whereas the terminal already marks tabs the user has not visited (iTerm2 activity dot, tmux window activity flag), which is a strictly better unread signal because it tracks actual attention rather than guessing from a timestamp.
impactAttack: Nothing is at risk. A finished session output sits in its transcript and its changes sit in the worktree, retrievable at any time; discovering it two hours later costs delay, not loss, so the prevents-concrete-loss band does not apply. Decisively, the user next action is identical under both of the labels E1 currently lumps together: open the pane and read it. Splitting reward from chore reorders a queue and does not change a decision. The claim that splitting the two is the entire value is an aesthetic claim about the board, not a behavioural one about the user.

accessAttack: This is neither information nor unavailable. The note says calm mode attention sort is most of the answer already, so the honest access score is one click in a place the user knows to look: a toggle that ships in 0.6.0 today. Scoring 72 prices the engineering work of changing a default and porting it to the card view as though it were the user cost of obtaining the ranking. Without Cargento at all, the ranking inputs are per-pane facts and the ordering of 3-12 rows is one visual sweep over a list. The move from 8 to 72 in the realignment, plus 64, is the largest single unexplained jump on a pure presentation item.
impactAttack: A dozen rows do not need machine ordering: a blocked row is already visually distinct with a badge, and the eye finds it in one pass. The failure the board names, dealing with the thing that I see, is a discipline failure, and a default sort does not impose discipline — the user still clicks what they feel like clicking. Worse, correct urgency ordering requires stakes, and D8 on this same board concedes stakes cannot be inferred reliably and that wrong inferred stakes are worse than none. A ranking that cannot know which task matters is convenience wearing a confident face, and it is the same objection the author accepted for D8 and declined to apply here.

accessAttack: The evidence offered is the refutation. The ritual is quoted verbatim because the user performs it today, unaided: pause the job, type summarise what you have done and give me a prompt for a follow-up session. That is one sentence, comfortably under 30 seconds, and its trigger is the quota figure the same board scores at access 12. The harnesses also ship most of the mechanism already: /compact and automatic compaction, claude --continue and --resume, codex resume. Access 62 is DEC-2 write path plus A1 integration priced as user effort, which is the exact failure mode the review notes admit to. A demonstrated manual workaround is proof of low access by definition — you cannot cite the user doing it by hand as evidence that they cannot.
impactAttack: It automates the cheapest step of the pain and leaves the pain. The loss is being force-paused mid-job and surrendering two hours to the reset; E7 does not prevent the pause, it drafts the handover paragraph the user was going to write anyway. Where it fires it is bounded by trigger accuracy: early and it truncates work that would have finished, late and it is useless. And a handoff prompt composed without the user judgement about what matters next is exactly the artifact people rewrite, which returns the saving to zero. Demonstrated demand proves the ritual is wanted; it does not prove that removing 30 seconds of typing from it is worth 81.

accessAttack: Self-refuting in its own note: its information difficulty is exactly A1 difficulty, because it reads the same number — and A1 is scored 12. The route is /usage in Claude Code, which returns both windows and both reset times in one command, or for a Barista user the 5-hour percentage already sitting in the status line unprompted, with no command at all. Composing two printed numbers into a go or no-go is a judgement the user makes inside the same glance. 68 is the design work of collapsing the usage cluster into one indicator, priced as the user access cost. This is the cleanest synthesis-inflation case on the board: every input is 12 to 18, the composite is 68, and the note states outright that no new source is involved.
impactAttack: The light is either redundant or wrong. At 15 percent used it says what the number said; at 90 percent it says what the number said. In the ambiguous middle the answer depends entirely on how large the job is, and Cargento cannot know that: A6, overrun likelihood before you start, is rated difficulty 88 and called speculative by the same author. So the indicator guesses precisely where it would add value, and a red light that is wrong twice teaches the user to open the underlying percentage, which is A1 again. Behaviourally, someone who sat down to start a big job starts it; dashboards rarely revoke permission a developer has already granted themselves.
